decks.title: Python Fundamentals — Part 1: Tokens, Variables, Data Types and Operators
goals: Describe the features of Python and use interactive and script mode
Identify tokens, write valid identifiers and explain variables, l-values and r-values
Name the data types, tell mutable from immutable objects, and use arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, identity and membership operators

slides.heading: Python Fundamentals
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **tokens**, **variables**, **data types** and **operators**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: features and tokens, variables and comments, data types, mutable and immutable objects, and operators
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to Python. In this first part we learn what a Python program is made of. We meet tokens, variables and data types, and we find out which objects can be changed and which cannot. Then we study the operators that combine values. Every output you see in these slides was produced by running real Python code.

slides.heading: Features of Python
slides.body_md: Python is an **interpreted**, **high-level**, **dynamically typed** language.

rows: Statements are translated and run one at a time, so errors show up quickly
Close to English; no need to manage memory or hardware
No declarations: the type belongs to the object, not to the name
Total and total are two different names
Open source, and the same program runs on many systems

visual.alt: Table of five features of Python: interpreted, high-level, dynamically typed, case-sensitive, and free and portable, each with what it means

slides.narration: Python is interpreted, which means statements are translated and run one at a time. It is high level, so it reads almost like English. It is dynamically typed, so we never declare a type. And it is case sensitive. Because it is free and runs on many systems, it is an excellent first language.

slides.heading: Interactive mode and script mode
slides.body_md: Use **interactive mode** to try ideas and **script mode** to keep programs.

rows: In a file saved with the extension .py
The whole file from the first line to the last
Only when the program prints it
Programs you want to keep and run again

visual.alt: Comparison table of interactive mode and script mode: where you type, how the code runs, when a value is shown, and what each is best for

slides.narration: There are two ways to run Python. In interactive mode you type one statement at the prompt and the answer appears at once, even without print. In script mode you save the program in a file and run it as a whole, and a value appears only when the program prints it. Choose interactive for quick trials.

slides.heading: Character set and tokens
slides.body_md: A program is made of **tokens**: the smallest units that have a meaning.

rows: Reserved word with a fixed meaning
A fixed value written in the program

visual.alt: Table of the five kinds of tokens: keyword, identifier, literal, operator and punctuator, each with its meaning and examples
visual.caption: The character set is the set of letters, digits and symbols that tokens are made of.

slides.narration: Every program is written with letters, digits and symbols, which together are the character set. These are grouped into tokens. A keyword is a reserved word. An identifier is a name you choose. A literal is a fixed value. An operator works on values, and a punctuator such as a bracket or a colon gives the code its structure.

slides.heading: Identifiers and keywords
slides.body_md: An identifier uses **letters, digits and underscores**, must not **start with a digit** and must not be a **keyword**.

visual.alt: Table that tests six names as identifiers: total_fee Yes, 2nd_bus No, fee-paid No, class No, Fee Yes, my name No; each tested by assigning a value to it
visual.caption: Validity checked by running an assignment to each name.

slides.narration: The rules for identifiers are simple. Use letters, digits and the underscore. Never start with a digit. Never use a space or a symbol such as the hyphen, because the hyphen is the minus operator. And never use a keyword. Capital letters are allowed, but remember that Fee and fee are different names.

slides.heading: Quick check: valid identifier
slides.body_md: Choose the valid name.
slides.narration: Apply the rules for identifiers to each choice. Remember that a name may not start with a digit and may not contain a space or a hyphen.

slides.heading: Variables, l-value and r-value
slides.body_md: A **variable** is a name that refers to an object. In an assignment the **right side is worked out first**.

visual.alt: Table of three assignment statements showing the l-value, the r-value and the value stored in the variable
visual.caption: The right side is worked out first, then the result is stored in the name on the left.

slides.narration: A variable is a name bound to an object. In an assignment, the name on the left is the l-value, and the expression on the right is the r-value. Python works out the right side first and then binds the result to the name. So a statement such as rate equals rate plus three is perfectly sensible. Comments begin with a hash sign and are ignored.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: tracing assignments
slides.body_md:
Follow each statement and write the values.

```python
a = 6
b = a + 4
a = a * b
b = a - b
a, b = b, a
```

visual.alt: Trace table of five assignment statements; after the last statement a is 50 and b is 60
visual.caption: A dash means the variable does not exist yet. The last statement swaps the values.

slides.narration: Trace these five statements one at a time. Each statement uses the current values of the names on its right side. The last statement swaps the two names in a single step, so the values of a and b change places. A trace table like this is the safest way to find the output of a program.

slides.heading: Data types
slides.body_md: Every value has a **type**. The type name is found with `type(value).__name__`.

visual.alt: Table of nine literals with the type name Python reports and whether the type is mutable: 42 is int, 3.75 is float, 4 + 2j is complex, True is bool, "Isha" is str, [3, 6] is list, (3, 6) is tuple, {"pen": 5} is dict, None is NoneType
visual.caption: Type names found with type(...).__name__.

slides.narration: Python has numbers of type int, float and complex, the truth values of type bool, text of type str, and the collections list, tuple and dict. The special value None stands for no value. The table shows the type name that Python itself reports for each literal, and whether the type is mutable.

slides.heading: Quick check: literals and types
slides.body_md: Match each literal with its type.
slides.narration: Remember that a number in quote marks is text, not a number, and that True and False belong to the type bool.

slides.heading: Mutable and immutable objects
slides.body_md: A **mutable** object can be changed in place; an **immutable** object cannot.

rows: `TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment`
`TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment`

visual.alt: Table that tries to change an item of a list, a dictionary, a tuple and a string; the list and dictionary change, the tuple and string raise a TypeError
visual.caption: Results produced by running each change.

slides.narration: A list and a dictionary are mutable, so we can change their items in place. Numbers, strings and tuples are immutable. Trying to assign to an item of a tuple or a string stops the program with a type error. To get a different value from an immutable object, we build a new object instead.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: two names, one list
slides.body_md:
Does changing one name change the other?

```python
plan = ["Maths", "Art"]
copy = plan
copy.append("Music")
copy = copy + ["Yoga"]
```

visual.alt: Trace table of a list and a second name; after the append both names show the same three subjects, but after copy is rebuilt with plus, plan is ['Maths', 'Art', 'Music'] and copy is ['Maths', 'Art', 'Music', 'Yoga']
visual.caption: Rows produced by running the statements and testing with is.

slides.narration: In this example a second name is bound to the same list. Because a list is mutable, append changes the shared object, and both names show the new subject. But joining with plus builds a brand new list. The second name is then bound to that new list, and the two names no longer refer to the same object.

slides.heading: Quick check: mutable object
slides.body_md: Which object can be changed in place?
slides.narration: Think about which of these types allows its items to be changed after it has been created.

slides.heading: Arithmetic operators
slides.body_md: Seven operators work on numbers. Note that `/` always gives a **float**.

visual.alt: Table of the seven arithmetic operators with an example and its value: 17 + 5 is 22, 17 - 5 is 12, 17 * 5 is 85, 17 / 5 is 3.4, 17 // 5 is 3, 17 % 5 is 2, 17 ** 2 is 289

slides.narration: The arithmetic operators are plus, minus, times, true division, floor division, modulus and exponentiation. True division always gives a float. Floor division gives the whole part of the quotient, rounded down. The modulus gives the remainder. And the double star raises a number to a power.

slides.heading: Relational and logical operators
slides.body_md: Relational operators compare; `and`, `or` and `not` combine the answers.

visual.alt: Table of relational and logical expressions with their values: 7 > 5 is True, 7 == 7.0 is True, 7 != 5 is True, 7 <= 5 is False, 7 > 5 and 5 > 9 is False, 7 > 5 or 5 > 9 is True, not 7 > 5 is False
visual.caption: Relational operators give True or False; and, or, not combine those answers.

slides.narration: Relational operators compare two values and give true or false. Notice that seven double equals seven point zero is true, because only the values are compared. The logical operators and, or and not combine true and false answers. And is true only when both sides are true, while or is true when at least one side is true.

slides.heading: Assignment and augmented assignment
slides.body_md: An **augmented assignment** such as `n += 3` updates the variable in one step.

visual.alt: Table of six augmented assignment operators applied to n equal to 20 with the operand 3, giving 23, 17, 60, 6, 2, 8000
visual.caption: Values produced by running each statement on n = 20.

slides.narration: A single equals sign assigns a value. An augmented assignment combines an operator with the assignment and updates the same variable. Plus equals adds, star equals multiplies, and double slash equals does floor division. Each statement in the table was run on a variable that starts at twenty.

slides.heading: Quick check: augmented assignment
slides.body_md: Predict the output.
slides.narration: Apply the three updates one after another. Each statement works on the value left by the previous one.

slides.heading: Identity and membership operators
slides.body_md: `==` compares **values**; `is` compares **objects**; `in` tests whether an item is present.

visual.alt: Table of identity and membership expressions after two equal lists and a second name for the first; values: q == r is True, q is r is False, q is s is True, q is not r is True, 4 in q is True, 5 not in q is True, "ab" in "cabin" is True
visual.caption: Setup: q and r are equal lists; s is another name for q.

slides.narration: The identity operators is and is not ask whether two names refer to the very same object. Double equals only asks whether the values are equal. Two equal lists made separately are not the same object. The membership operators in and not in test whether an item is present in a list or a text.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: letters, digits, underscore; not a digit first; not a keyword; case-sensitive
a name bound to an object; the type belongs to the object
int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, dict, None
list and dict change in place; the others cannot
arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, identity, membership

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: tokens, identifiers, variables, data types, mutable types and operators

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. A program is made of tokens. Identifiers follow simple rules and are case sensitive. A variable is a name bound to an object, and the type belongs to the object. Lists and dictionaries are mutable. Python has arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, identity and membership operators.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: List the **five kinds of tokens** with one example of each.
For identifiers, check three things: the first character, the characters used, and whether it is a **keyword**.
Remember `/` gives a **float**, `//` rounds **down** and `%` has the sign of the divisor.
Do not confuse `==` (same value) with `is` (same object).
Show a **trace table** whenever the output depends on several updates.
slides.narration: Some advice for the exam. Learn the five kinds of tokens with an example of each. Check identifiers by their first character, their other characters and whether they are keywords. Remember that true division gives a float and floor division rounds down. Do not confuse double equals with is. And draw a trace table whenever several updates are involved.

decks.title: Python Fundamentals — Part 2: Expressions, Type Conversion, Input/Output and Errors
goals: Evaluate expressions using precedence and associativity, and tell an expression from a statement
Convert types implicitly and explicitly, and use input() and print() with sep and end
Recognise syntax, run-time and logical errors and read an error message

slides.heading: Expressions, conversion, input and errors
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **evaluating**, **converting**, **reading and printing**, and **debugging**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: expressions and precedence, type conversion, print and input, kinds of errors, and debugging
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we put the operators to work. We learn the order in which Python evaluates an expression, how types are converted, how a program reads input and prints output, and how to recognise the three kinds of error. Try each example in your own editor as you go.

slides.heading: Expressions and statements
slides.body_md: An **expression** produces a value. A **statement** is a complete instruction.

visual.alt: Table that tells expressions from statements: an expression produces a value, a statement carries out an action; four examples with what happens
visual.caption: An expression produces a value; a statement is a complete instruction.

slides.narration: An expression is a combination of values and operators that produces a value. A statement is a complete instruction that Python carries out, such as an assignment or a call to print. An assignment statement stores a value and shows nothing. A statement can contain an expression, but an expression on its own does not do anything in a script.

slides.heading: Precedence of operators
slides.body_md: When operators are mixed, the one with **higher priority** is applied first. Equal priority goes **left to right**.

visual.alt: Table of operator priority from highest to lowest: brackets, exponent, unary signs, multiply divide floor-divide modulus, add subtract, comparisons, not, and, or

slides.narration: Python follows a fixed order. Brackets come first, then the exponent, then the unary signs. Then multiplication, the two divisions and the modulus share one level, and addition and subtraction share the next. Comparisons come after the arithmetic, then not, then and, and finally or. When in doubt, use brackets.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: evaluating an expression
slides.body_md:
Evaluate step by step.

```python
print(8 + 3 * 2 ** 3 // 4 - 10 % 4)
```

visual.alt: Step table for evaluating 8 + 3 * 2 ** 3 // 4 - 10 % 4: 2 ** 3 is 8, 3 * 8 is 24, 24 // 4 is 6, 10 % 4 is 2, 8 + 6 is 14, 14 - 2 is 12; the final value is 12
visual.caption: Final value of 8 + 3 * 2 ** 3 // 4 - 10 % 4: 12.

slides.narration: Let us evaluate a long expression. The exponent has the highest priority, so two to the power three comes first. Then multiplication, floor division and modulus are applied from left to right. Only then do we add and subtract, again from left to right. Each result in the table was worked out by Python itself.

slides.heading: Quick check: order of evaluation
slides.body_md: Put the steps in order.
slides.narration: Decide which operator is applied first, then which comes next. Remember that plus and minus are applied last.

slides.heading: Associativity and tricky cases
slides.body_md: The exponent works **right to left**. Floor division and `%` need care with **negative** numbers.

rows: ** is applied before the minus sign
Floor division rounds down, towards minus infinity
The remainder takes the sign of the divisor

visual.alt: Table of six tricky expressions: 64 / 8 / 2 is 4.0, 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512, -3 ** 2 is -9, (-3) ** 2 is 9, -17 // 5 is -4, -17 % 5 is 3
visual.caption: Every value was produced by running the expression.

slides.narration: Most operators work from left to right, but the exponent works from right to left. A minus sign in front of a number is applied after the exponent. With negative numbers, floor division rounds down, towards minus infinity, and the remainder takes the sign of the divisor. Test such cases before you rely on them.

slides.heading: Implicit type conversion
slides.body_md: When types are mixed, Python **promotes** to the wider type automatically.

visual.alt: Table of implicit conversion: 5 + 2.0 gives 7.0 of type float; 5 + True gives 6 of type int; 5 + 2j gives (5+2j) of type complex; True + True gives 2 of type int; 7 / 2 gives 3.5 of type float
visual.caption: Python promotes to the wider type: bool, then int, then float, then complex.

slides.narration: In implicit conversion, Python changes the type for you. A bool counts as an int, an int mixed with a float becomes a float, and a float mixed with a complex number becomes complex. The result always has the widest type in the expression. True division always gives a float, even for whole numbers.

slides.heading: Explicit type conversion
slides.body_md: In **explicit conversion**, the programmer calls `int()`, `float()`, `str()` or `bool()`.

rows: `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.7'`

visual.alt: Table of explicit conversion calls with their results: int(7.9) gives 7; int("42") gives 42; float(3) gives 3.0; float("2.5") gives 2.5; str(15) + "0" gives 150; bool(0) gives False; int("3.7") gives ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.7'
visual.caption: The last call fails because int() accepts only a string that spells a whole number.

slides.narration: In explicit conversion, also called type casting, we call a function. Int cuts off the decimal part of a float. Int and float can read a number from a string. Str turns a number into text, so plus then joins two texts. A string that does not spell a whole number cannot be passed to int, and Python reports a value error.

slides.heading: Quick check: a conversion error
slides.body_md: Which statement causes a ValueError?
slides.narration: Remember that int can read a string only when the string spells a whole number.

slides.heading: Output with print(): sep and end
slides.body_md: `sep` sets what goes **between** values; `end` sets what comes **after** the last value.

visual.alt: Table of print calls with sep and end and their exact output: print("Rs", 40) shows Rs 40; print("Rs", 40, sep="") shows Rs40; print("12", "05", "26", sep="-") shows 12-05-26; print("Go", end="!"); print("Stop") shows Go!Stop
visual.caption: sep goes between the values; end goes after the last one.

slides.narration: The print function separates its values by a single space and ends with a new line. The sep argument changes the separator, and an empty text joins the values. The end argument changes what is added after the last value. With end set to an exclamation mark, the next print continues on the same line.

slides.heading: Input with input()
slides.body_md: `input()` **always returns a string**. Convert it before arithmetic.

rows: `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '2.5'`
`ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'`
`ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'abc'`

visual.alt: Table showing that input() always returns a string, and what int() and float() do to the typed text: 25 gives 25 with int and 25.0 with float; 2.5 gives ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '2.5' with int and 2.5 with float; abc gives ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc' with int and ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'abc' with float
visual.caption: Error lines were produced by running the conversions.

slides.narration: Whatever the user types, input gives back a string. To do arithmetic, convert it with int or float. Int accepts only a whole number in the text, so a typed decimal point makes it fail. Float accepts both. Text that is not a number at all fails with both functions.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a pay program
slides.body_md:
Read a name, a rate and some hours, and print the pay.

```python
name = input()
rate = float(input())
hours = int(input())
pay = rate * hours
print(name, "earns", pay)
```

visual.alt: Trace table of a pay program for the typed values Meera, 300 and 8; pay becomes 2400 and the program prints Meera earns 2400.0
visual.caption: Typed values are shown inside the statements; the program prints: Meera earns 2400.0

slides.narration: Here is a complete program with input and output. The name stays text, the rate is converted to a float and the hours to an int. The pay is the product, which is a float. The final print joins the three values with spaces. The table shows each variable after each statement for the typed values.

slides.heading: Quick check: print and sep
slides.body_md: Predict the output.
slides.narration: With an empty separator, no space is placed between the values. Join them exactly as they are.

slides.heading: Three kinds of error
slides.body_md: A **syntax** error stops the program before it starts, a **run-time** error stops it while it runs, and a **logical** error gives a wrong answer silently.

rows: `ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero`
Never: the answer is just wrong
Prints `70.0`, not the mean of 40 and 60

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of error: syntax error found before running, run-time error found while running, and logical error that gives no message but a wrong answer; each with an example and what you see

slides.narration: There are three kinds of error. A syntax error breaks the rules of the language, and Python reports it before running anything. A run-time error happens while a valid statement is being carried out, such as dividing by zero. A logical error gives no message at all, only a wrong answer, so it is the hardest to find.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: reading error messages
slides.body_md: The **last line** of an error message names the error and says what went wrong.

rows: `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`
`ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fifty'`
`SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Perhaps you forgot a comma?`

visual.alt: Table of five faulty statements with the last line of the error message: NameError: name 'total' is not defined; TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str; ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fifty'; ZeroDivisionError: division by zero; SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Perhaps you forgot a comma?
visual.caption: Read the last line first: it names the error and says what went wrong.

slides.narration: Always read the last line of an error message first. A name error means a name has no value. A type error means two types cannot be combined, for example a string and a number. A value error means the type is right but the value is not. A zero division error and a syntax error have their own clear messages.

slides.heading: Debugging
slides.body_md: **Debugging** is finding and fixing errors. Always compare the output with a hand calculation.

nodes.label: Read the last line of the message

visual.alt: Debugging flow: read the last line of the message, find the line number, fix the statement, run again, and check the answer against a hand calculation
visual.caption: A logical error gives no message, so the last step matters most.

slides.narration: To debug, read the last line of the message, find the line number, fix the statement and run again. A logical error gives no message, so check the output against a small example that you work out by hand. Fix one error at a time, and run the program after each fix.

slides.heading: Quick check: when is an error found?
slides.body_md: Which problem appears only while the program runs?
slides.narration: Think about which of these problems Python can detect before it starts running the program, and which only when a statement is carried out.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: produces a value; a statement is an instruction
Python promotes to the wider type (bool, int, float, complex)
int(), float(), str(), bool() called by the programmer
sep goes between values; end goes after the last value
always returns a string; convert it before arithmetic
syntax (before running), run-time (while running), logical (wrong answer)

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: expressions, precedence, implicit and explicit conversion, print, input and the three kinds of error

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. An expression produces a value. Precedence decides the order of evaluation. Types are converted implicitly or explicitly. Print has the sep and end arguments, and input always returns a string. Syntax errors are found before running, run-time errors while running, and logical errors only by checking the answer.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Apply the **priority order** and write each step of an evaluation.
Convert `input()` with **`int()` or `float()`** before any arithmetic.
Say whether a conversion is **implicit** (done by Python) or **explicit** (called by you).
Name an error **and** its cause, then write the corrected statement.
For `print()` outputs, mark where **sep** and **end** change the usual spacing and new lines.
slides.narration: Some advice for the exam. Apply the priority order and write each step. Convert input with int or float before any arithmetic. State whether a conversion is implicit or explicit. When asked about an error, name it, give its cause and write the corrected statement. And for print questions, watch where sep and end change the spacing and the new lines.

sections.heading: 1. Python, modes and tokens
sections.body_md:
Python is an **interpreted**, **high-level**, **dynamically typed** and **case-sensitive** language. It is free and runs on many systems.

**Interactive mode** runs one statement at a time at the `>>>` prompt and shows the value of an expression at once. **Script mode** runs a whole program saved in a `.py` file; a value is shown only when the program prints it.

A program is written with a **character set** (letters, digits and symbols) and is made of **tokens**: keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuators.

key_terms.definition_md: The smallest unit of a program that has a meaning: keyword, identifier, literal, operator or punctuator.
A reserved word with a fixed meaning, such as while; it cannot be used as a name.
A fixed value written directly in the program, such as 42 or "Isha".

rows: Statements are translated and run one at a time, so errors show up quickly
Close to English; no need to manage memory or hardware
No declarations: the type belongs to the object, not to the name
Total and total are two different names
Open source, and the same program runs on many systems

sections.heading: 2. Identifiers, variables and comments
sections.body_md:
An **identifier** is a name chosen by the programmer. It may use letters, digits and underscores, must not start with a digit, must not contain spaces or symbols, and must not be a keyword. Identifiers are case-sensitive.

A **variable** is a name that refers to an object. In `fare = rate * 5` the name on the left is the **l-value** and the expression on the right is the **r-value**; the right side is worked out first, so `rate = rate + 3` is valid. Every object has an **identity**, a **type** and a **value**.

A **comment** starts with `#` and runs to the end of the line; Python ignores it.

key_terms.definition_md: A programmer-chosen name for a variable or other object.
The name on the left of an assignment, which receives the value.
The value or expression on the right of an assignment.

visual.alt: Table that tests six names as identifiers: total_fee Yes, 2nd_bus No, fee-paid No, class No, Fee Yes, my name No; each tested by assigning a value to it
visual.caption: Validity checked by running an assignment to each name.

visuals.alt: Table of three assignment statements showing the l-value, the r-value and the value stored in the variable
visuals.caption: The right side is worked out first, then the result is stored in the name on the left.

visuals.alt: Trace table of five assignment statements; after the last statement a is 50 and b is 60
visuals.caption: A dash means the variable does not exist yet. The last statement swaps the values.

sections.heading: 3. Data types, mutable and immutable
sections.body_md:
The data types in this chapter are `int`, `float`, `complex`, `bool`, `str`, `list`, `tuple`, `dict` and the special value `None` (no value, type `NoneType`). Use `type(value).__name__` to see a type name.

A **mutable** object (list, dict) can be changed in place. An **immutable** object (int, float, complex, bool, str, tuple) cannot: an apparent change builds a new object and rebinds the name.

Two names can refer to the same mutable object, so a change made through one name is seen through the other.

key_terms.definition_md: An object whose contents can be changed in place, such as a list or dictionary.
An object that cannot be changed after it is created, such as a number, string or tuple.
The type belongs to the object, so a name may refer to objects of different types at different times.

sections.heading: 4. Operators
sections.body_md:
**Arithmetic:** `+ - * / // % **`. `/` always gives a float; `//` rounds down; `%` is the remainder; `**` is the power.

**Relational:** `< <= > >= == !=` give `True` or `False`. **Logical:** `and`, `or`, `not`.

**Assignment:** `=` and the **augmented** forms `+= -= *= /= //= %= **=`, which update a variable in one step.

**Identity:** `is`, `is not` (same object?). **Membership:** `in`, `not in` (is the item present?). `==` compares values; `is` compares objects.

sections.heading: 5. Expressions, precedence and type conversion
sections.body_md:
An **expression** produces a value; a **statement** is a complete instruction. The order of evaluation is: brackets, `**` (right to left), unary signs, `* / // %`, `+ -`, comparisons with `is` and `in`, `not`, `and`, `or`; operators of equal priority go left to right.

**Implicit conversion** is done by Python: the result is promoted to the wider type (bool, int, float, complex). **Explicit conversion** (type casting) is done by calling `int()`, `float()`, `str()` or `bool()`. `int("3.7")` fails with a `ValueError`.
